W1-1.note: The search ends in disappointment that gives way to feeling he 'touched hands' with a long-dead boy comrade; E is only a passing thought.

W1-2.note: The capitals name the words that strike a 'chord' that 'never fails to thrill'; CAVE, TRAP-DOOR and SLIDING-PANEL are not riches, so D fits only half the list.

W1-3.note: The foreign coins were 'thicker and clumsier of make than those I hoarded myself.'

W1-4.note: He calls the earlier boy a 'kindred spirit' and 'my little comrade,' and warmth comes back to his heart.

W1-5.note: 'Some other boy, perhaps, would some day release that spring again. I trusted he would be equally appreciative.'

W1-6.note: The noisy game of bears or bandits is just getting going, so 'up' means under way; students who know 'the game is up' will pick C.

W2-1.note: The passage moves from 'a strange man' to 'He is my father'; the ending rules out the 'lasting' distance in E.

W2-2.note: The paragraph shows a world 'bounded by the wooded hills of a little Wisconsin coulee,' with only darkness beyond it.

W2-3.note: He submitted 'rather for the reason that my mother urged me forward than because of any affection.'

W2-4.note: The text notes she was 'two years older than I' and right after says 'I had forgotten him—the baby had never known him', which implies that age is why she remembered him.

W2-5.note: 'Of her own motion' means by her own choice, set against the narrator, who had to be urged forward.

W2-6.note: He still hears 'the sad reproach' in the voice and reflects that the war 'had come between this patriot and his sons.'

W3-1.note: Both rescue the nest, then never go back to see whether the birds lived; B fails because 'twas no make-believe' from the start.

W3-2.note: 'The cutter-bar had just gone champing over' the nest, leaving it 'defenseless to the heat and light.'

W3-3.note: The chicks rising as if to a late mother-bird 'Made me ask would the mother-bird return.'

W3-4.note: The speaker's fond 'You were forever finding some new play' and the offer to 'help pretend' show warmth toward the companion.

W3-5.note: 'Dared not spare to do' means did not dare hold back from doing, so neglect is closest; D draws on 'can't spare' (can't afford), and a careful reader could argue it.

W3-6.note: 'We turned to other things' and the shared 'have you?' show surprise that their care stopped, not blame or a hint that the birds died.

W4-1.note: The Labor Museum leads Angelina to see her mother against a background other than the tenement, and to take pride in her.

W4-2.note: They could 'drop their spindles over the edge of a precipice,' which built skill beyond the neighboring towns.

W4-3.note: 'Traditional ... observances' that her religion clung to are customs and practices.

W4-4.note: The paragraph is what the author 'could not convey to the child, but upon which my own mind persistently dwelt': the mother torn from everything she knew.

W4-5.note: The author dwells on the mother being 'torn from it all' and walking 'timidly but with poignant sensibility' on a strange shore.

W4-6.note: 'The thought of her mother with any other background than that of the tenement was new to Angelina.'

W5-1.note: The author argues the squirrel is the most 'influential' animal and lays out 'how substantial a foundation' that claim has; A and E are only parts of the case.

W5-2.note: Though only a few inches long, the squirrel 'makes himself more important than even the huge bears.'

W5-3.note: 'The greater portion is of course stored away for food to last during the winter and spring'; only 'some' are buried singly.

W5-4.note: He gives the facts 'to show upon how substantial a foundation the importance I ascribe to him rests', which pre-empts doubt about a large claim for a small animal.

W5-5.note: 'Closely allied' is about kinship, since the next sentence calls the squirrel a possible 'lineal descendant.'

W5-6.note: He calls it 'the most interesting and influential' animal, the 'master-existence' and 'master forester,' and 'the larger and more beautiful animal.'

W6-1.note: The passage asks 'what's going on here?' about the missing foliage and answers with the plume, Kona winds, SO2 and tephra.

W6-2.note: The dominant Northeast trade winds carried the plumes Southwest into the Kaʻū Desert, away from the viewing areas.

W6-3.note: The pH figures come from samples 'collected downwind of Kīlauea's summit' in 2008-2018 and show how acidic the rain was, not readings from 2026.

W6-4.note: The author calls it 'a secret weapon' and 'the amazing capability.'

W6-5.note: 'Hearty native trees' (meaning hardy) are trees 'highly adapted to survive' harsh volcanic conditions.

W6-6.note: Tephra seems light, yet 'it has enough energy to strip the foliage right off the trees'; C goes against its lightness, and the acid gas is a separate blow.
